performers: Pierre Mollet, baritone; women of the Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: Pierre Mollet sings a psalm of persecution and defiance, after an orchestral opening marked Grave, rude. Boulanger saves the women’s voices for the close, where celesta, harp and muted strings surround them.

sections.label: Intro · Winds above plucked basses
sections.mNote: Accented woodwind and horn chords begin the D-minor psalm

sections.label: A · The baritone’s first appeal
sections.mNote: The voice holds while descending figures run through the strings

sections.label: B · Triplets in the clarinets
sections.mNote: Clarinets ripple above the slower bass and vocal line

sections.label: Coda · Women’s voices and celesta
sections.mNote: The women enter softly above harp and muted strings

cues.title: Grave and rough
cues.text: Grave, rude: solemn and rough. The woodwinds and horns press accents into their long chords, while double basses pluck beneath them. Violins, violas and cellos wait. Boulanger gives the orchestra thirty bars before a voice sings.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, plate D. & F. 10382 (1924), p. 1 and orchestral introduction through p. 7. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP829067-PMLP430945-Boulanger,_L_-_Psalm_129_full_score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mollet takes up the words
cues.text: Pierre Mollet’s baritone gives words to the orchestra’s anger: the psalm speaks of oppression endured since youth. While the voice holds its notes, descending figures run from the violins down through the violas and cellos to the double basses.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 8, figure 3: opening vocal phrase and descending string figures. The score permits solo baritone in place of the printed male-chorus parts; Mollet is credited on this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Furrows in the back
cues.text: The psalm’s image is brutal: ploughmen cut furrows into the speaker’s back. Clarinets and bass clarinet move up and down in triplets. Beneath them, the bass rises slowly while the voice draws out its complaint.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 11, figure 4, setting Des laboureurs ont labouré mon dos; clarinet triplets and rising lower parts. Helen Julia Minors, preface (2011). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A concert without the composer
cues.text: In 1921 Henri Büsser conducts the first performance at the Salle Pleyel in Paris, for the Concerts Dandelot. Boulanger has been dead for three years. The score she finishes in Rome in 1916 is only now reaching its first audience.
cues.evidence: Helen Julia Minors, preface to Psalm 129 (Musikproduktion Höflich, 2011), gives the 1916 composition and 1921 première. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1100.html

cues.title: The women enter softly
cues.text: The coda slows. Women’s voices enter on a wordless vowel, high above the continuing prayer; flute and celesta trace their line. The strings put on mutes. Harp notes move gently beneath chords that still rub against one another.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 22–24, figure 8: Un peu plus lent, women’s voices marked ppp on Ah, flute, celesta, harp and muted strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The words run out
cues.text: The final vocal phrase has no words. Soft chords hang in the divided strings, with small replies from horn, bassoon and harp. The dissonances remain in place as the last notes die away.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 25, final four bars: wordless voices, sustained divided strings and solo instrumental replies. Helen Julia Minors’s preface describes the unresolved closing dissonances.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The orchestra acquires words
transitions.how: The opening chords return beneath the first vocal phrase, marked a Tempo, grave et rude. The winds hold their accented harmony while the strings launch quick figures. As the baritone holds the end of his phrase, a five-note run passes down the string sections to the double basses.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 7–8, figure 3; Helen Julia Minors (2011) identifies the return of the introduction’s chord progression beneath the voice.

transitions.title: Clarinets begin their triplets
transitions.how: At figure 4 the clarinets and bass clarinet begin continuous triplets. Bassoons, horns, harp and low strings rise more slowly beneath them. The baritone also begins with a triplet, then stretches the words over the clarinets’ running notes; the vocal part is marked contenu, restrained.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), p. 11, figure 4: clarinet triplets, ascending bass and contenu vocal phrase.

transitions.title: Celesta and voices above the bass
transitions.how: Un peu plus lent slows the coda as the metre alternates between four crotchets and three minims. The bass drops in long notes beneath a quiet harp figure. Women’s voices, flute and celesta sing the upper line; the horns and strings are muted.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score (1924), pp. 21–22, figure 8: tempo and metre changes, descending bass, solo harp, women’s voices and celesta; muting instructions for horns and strings.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Psaume CXXIX, Durand full score (1924), plate D. & F. 10382
source.locator: Prefatory performance options and printed pp. 1, 5, 8, 11, 16, 21–25. The score permits a solo baritone with women’s voices, as on this recording. At figure 6 the baritone version reduces the trumpet and trombone parts. The orchestra includes two harps and sarrusophone.

timeline.note: Accented winds and horns sound above plucked double basses. The other strings rest.
Violins and cellos hold long notes while violas and clarinets repeat their shorter figures.
Pierre Mollet’s baritone enters at figure 3. Descending string figures answer the vocal phrase.
Clarinets and bass clarinet play triplets beneath the voice at figure 4.
The opening phrase returns at figure 6, with the voice marked clamant. The baritone version uses one trumpet and one trombone for the first six bars.
Women’s voices enter very softly at figure 8, with celesta and harp. The strings put on mutes.
The women hold wordless chords above muted strings. Harps, celesta and quiet winds carry the closing phrases.

fields.note: The sleeve names Mollet for this work and describes the women’s wordless closing voices. The score allows several alternatives; its male-chorus layout is not mistaken for the recorded solo version. The exact number of women and performing edition are unknown.

composer.epithet: At nineteen she won the Prix de Rome; before her death at twenty-four she had written songs of lost love and psalms that shake the room.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
At the Château de Compiègne in May 1913, five young composers were shut away writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Among the signatures was Lili Boulanger’s. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome. Illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the Académie des Beaux-Arts’ thirty-six voters supported her. Faust et Hélène gave them a tenor in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, all carried by a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
